actions.title: Session 1 recap: what design thinking is
Group task: prepare the HMW workshop

sources.title: Session 1 notes: what design thinking is
sources.text:
Design thinking is a human-centred way of solving problems. Teams start by understanding people before proposing solutions. The process moves through empathise, define, ideate, prototype and test, and teams often loop back when they learn something new.

The observation methods primer explains how to watch people doing a task in their own setting. Note what they do, what tools they use and where they pause. Record what you saw separately from what you think it means.

The session 1 recap takes about fifteen minutes. The primer reading takes about twenty minutes and must be read before the session 2 exercise and the reading check quiz.

sources.title: Session 2 notes: observing users
sources.text:
Session 2 practised observation. Extreme users, people with very high or very low use of a product, often reveal needs that average users hide. Analogies from other industries help teams notice patterns.

The exercise asks for five observation notes. Each note should record time, place, action and a direct quote if the person agreed to be quoted. Do not record names. The exercise needs the session 2 recap and the observation primer first, and takes about thirty minutes.

sources.title: Session 3 notes: empathy mapping
sources.text:
An empathy map has four areas: says, does, thinks and feels. Says and does come from evidence you collected. Thinks and feels are interpretations and must be labelled as such, with the evidence that supports them.

The empathy map exercise takes about thirty-five minutes and builds on your observation notes from session 2. The reading check quiz covers the observation primer. In version 1 of the course page the quiz was due on 24 November at 18:00 Dubai time. Version 2 lists 26 November, and the coordinator has not yet confirmed which date is correct.

sources.title: Session 4 notes: problem framing
sources.text:
Problem framing turns research into a clear point-of-view statement: a user, a need and an insight. A good statement is specific enough to guide ideas but does not contain a solution.

Version 2 of the course adds a short framing case study reading of about fifteen minutes. The point-of-view exercise now takes about thirty minutes instead of twenty-five. It needs the session 4 recap and your empathy map.

sources.title: Session 5 notes: how might we
sources.text:
How might we questions reframe a point-of-view statement as an opportunity. They should be broad enough to allow many ideas and narrow enough to be useful. Teams generate many questions, then vote on the most promising.

The group task is to prepare the HMW workshop. It takes about forty minutes. The course page lists 8 December, but this date has not been verified by the coordinator. In version 2 the task also needs the framing case study reading.

sources.title: Session 6 notes: envisioning futures
sources.text:
Envisioning uses hill statements to describe a future outcome for a specific user, written as who, what and wow. Future-state journey maps show how the experience should feel after the change.

Version 1 asked for a short reflection log entry. Version 2 replaces it with a reflection journal in a new format, which takes about twenty-five minutes.

studio_examples.notice: FICTIONAL EXAMPLES ONLY. Invented to show how the studio works. Not interviews, not participants, not research data. Never cite these as findings.

notes.text: I missed session two because of a late shift. When I came back I opened the LMS, the group chat and my email, and none of them agreed on the quiz date. I spent twenty minutes just working out what I had missed. I felt behind before I even started. What I need is one place that tells me the next thing to do.

I keep a paper list of tasks, but it goes out of date when the course page changes. Last time I did a reading that had been removed. I asked a classmate instead of the coordinator because I did not want to bother anyone. I would trust a plan if it showed where each task came from.

Every week I answer the same three questions about deadlines. Students email me at midnight before a quiz. When a date changes I post an announcement, but people who were away never see it. I would like questions to arrive with the task they refer to, so I can answer once and point others to it.

notes.context: Fictional example: learner using a screen reader
notes.text: The course page has a big table of weeks and it takes me a long time to find the current one. I usually only have half an hour on the train. I just want to start something useful in that half hour. Visual timelines are hard for me unless there is a list version.
